cards.name: Developer tutorial / quickstart
cards.summary: A step-by-step walkthrough in which every command and code block runs as written, in order, on a stated setup, and the reader ends with a working result they can see. Good ones state prerequisites and versions first, show the expected output after each step, and explain only what the reader needs to take the next step.
use_for: SDK or API quickstart ('Create your first payment link with the Python SDK')
Codelab or workshop handout for a developer-relations launch
'Build X with Y' tutorial on a company engineering blog
Onboarding guide for an internal platform new engineers must use
avoid: Explaining concepts at length inside a step: keep each step to one action and one result, and link out to an explanation page.
Writing a tutorial when the reader already knows the tool and wants one task done: that is a how-to (genre:how_to_article) or a troubleshooting entry (genre:troubleshooting_guide).
Listing every option, flag and parameter: that is reference (genre:api_reference); a tutorial picks one path and sticks to it.

cards.goal: Run every step and reach the stated working result on the first try, then follow the next-step link.

structure.does: Names what the reader will build or do and with which tool ('Send your first WhatsApp template message with the X Python SDK'); one line under it says what works at the end.
Accounts, API keys, OS, runtime and package versions, prior knowledge assumed; a 'last tested with' line.
Create the project and install dependencies with the exact commands, then show the output that proves it worked.
Numbered steps, each = one imperative action, one complete code block, which file it goes in, the expected output, and at most 2-3 sentences of why.
The full run with the complete expected output: the 'it works' moment.
The errors a tester actually hit, exact error text then the fix.
Links to the concept explanation, the how-to for the next task and the API reference; optionally the full final code or repo link.

length.note: Prose words, excluding code. A quickstart is one path in 3-6 steps (low end); a concept-teaching tutorial or codelab runs longer. The number of steps the minimum working result needs sets the length, not a word target.

checklist: Does the prerequisites section name every runtime, package and account, with version numbers?
Does every step start with one imperative action (Install, Create, Run, Add)?
Is every code block complete enough to paste and run, with placeholders clearly marked (YOUR_API_KEY) and no '...' gaps?
Does every step that produces output show the expected output?
Is it clear which file each snippet goes into and where in that file?
Is the same term used for the same thing throughout (not 'project' in step 2 and 'workspace' in step 5)?
Is there a troubleshooting section quoting exact error text?
Does it end with next-step links rather than a recap of what was just done?
Are secrets shown only as placeholders, never as real-looking keys?
Has someone run it end to end from a clean machine or new account?
pitfalls: Untested steps: the writer's machine already had a dependency, so step 3 fails for a fresh reader. Run it in a clean container or new account and record the exact versions in prerequisites.
Silent steps like 'Configure the client': every step needs the literal command or code.
Version drift: an SDK method gets renamed and the tutorial breaks quietly. Pin versions and add 'Last tested with v2.3 on <date>'.
Copy-paste traps: smart quotes, line numbers or the shell prompt ($, >) inside the copyable block. Keep prompts and output outside the code the reader copies.
Teaching the whole product: a quickstart that detours into architecture loses the reader. One path; link the concept page.
For Indian developers, examples can use Rs amounts, +91 numbers and local services, but keep instructions in plain English and never translate code identifiers.

require.label: points to next steps
require.regex: (?i)next step|what's next|where to go next|learn more|आगे

cards.exemplar_brief: Quickstart for a Bengaluru payments-API startup: 'Create your first payment link with the Python SDK', for backend developers at Indian D2C brands who know Python but have never used the API; English; 700-1,100 words plus code; goal: a working payment link printed in the terminal, then a click through to the webhooks how-to.

verified.note: Clean one-path quickstart: versioned prerequisites, every step one imperative action with file and position named, pinned install with expected output, a real 'it works' run, four troubleshooting entries with exact error text, and the webhooks how-to as the first next-step link. Only nit: the sample customer number is a real-looking mobile number; use an obviously fake one. Clean-machine 'last tested' date correctly left as a placeholder.

cards.name: Devotional content (aarti, bhajan, stuti, vrat katha text)
cards.summary: Devotional text for Hindu and other faith audiences: aarti and chalisa texts with their meaning, original bhajans and stutis, vrat katha retellings, mantra explainers and festival lore. Good devotional writing quotes traditional texts exactly, marks what is scripture and what is retelling, and speaks with warmth and reverence without promising miracles.
use_for: Festival-day posts, reels and WhatsApp cards for a devotional page (Navratri, Chhath, Janmashtami)
Vrat katha retold for an app or a YouTube audio track
Verse-by-verse meaning of the Hanuman Chalisa or an aarti
Original bhajan or stuti lyrics for a devotional channel or singer
Temple history and darshan-guide copy for a trust or pilgrimage operator
avoid: Inventing verses, 'lost' stories or miracles and presenting them as scripture: name the source text and label any retelling or interpretation as such.
Promising results ('chant this 11 times and get the job'): describe the belief in the tradition's own terms ('bhakt maante hain...') and stop there.
Pasting lyrics of modern film or label bhajans: they are copyrighted; use traditional public-domain texts or write original lines.
Jokes or satire about a deity inside a devotional brief: wrong genre, and it can attract a legal complaint (comp:bns_defamation_speech).
Mixing sampradaya details (Vaishnava vs Shaiva practice, regional vrat dates) without checking: confirm with the client's panchang or priest.

cards.goal: Feel the bhakti bhaav and do the devotional act: recite, sing, keep the vrat, visit, or share it with family.

structure.does: Opens with the deity's name and a traditional salutation ('जय माता दी'), then one line naming the occasion or the text.
Which text and tradition this comes from and when it is recited (tithi, weekday, festival), so the reader can place it.
The traditional verses exactly as in a standard edition the client approves (Devanagari, with IAST or simple roman if the audience needs it), or the original bhajan/stuti. Keep verse numbers.
Bhavarth verse by verse in simple Hindi or English, or the katha retold scene by scene; mark clearly where interpretation begins.
Vidhi, samagri, timing, do's and don'ts as the tradition describes them, attributed to the named text or to the client's priest.
Blessing line or jaykara, then a gentle CTA (save it for the vrat day, share with family, follow for daily aarti).

length.note: A reel caption or festival card is 60-200 words; a full chalisa explainer with verse-by-verse meaning runs into thousands. The text being explained sets the length.

checklist: Are traditional verses word-for-word identical to a standard printed edition, with no paraphrase passed off as the original?
Is the source text named wherever a story, rule or benefit is attributed to scripture?
Is every retelling or interpretation marked as such?
Are dates, tithis and muhurat taken from the client's panchang, or left out?
Is there no promise of material results (job, money, cure) from a ritual?
Are deity names and Sanskrit terms spelled one consistent way throughout?
Is there nothing that belittles another deity, sampradaya or faith?
Do original lyrics avoid any line lifted from a copyrighted film or label bhajan?
Does it close with a jaykara, blessing or gentle CTA?
pitfalls: AI-made 'shlokas' that look like Sanskrit but exist in no text: never compose Sanskrit verse and attribute it. Quote a standard edition, or label new lines as an original composition.
Wrong vrat or festival dates: dates vary by region and panchang. Ask the client which calendar they follow, or leave the date out.
Sanskritised Hindi the audience can't follow: keep the verses as they are, but write the bhavarth in everyday Hindi (lang:hindustani_everyday).
Encyclopaedia tone: write as a bhakt speaking to bhakts, warm and personal, while keeping every fact accurate.
Hashtag-stuffed captions on a devotional post read as spam: 3-5 specific tags at most, after the text.
cards.exemplar_brief: Instagram + WhatsApp post for a Varanasi-based puja-booking app on day 1 of Shardiya Navratri (Maa Shailputri): one line of context, the traditional dhyana mantra quoted exactly in Devanagari with roman transliteration, a 4-line bhavarth in simple Hindi, a 3-line vidhi, a jaykara and a soft CTA to book a Navratri puja; Hindi (Devanagari); 150-250 words.

verified.note: The Shailputri dhyana mantra matches the standard printed text; the IAST is serviceable but mixes conventions (vanchhita, mid-line capital). Bhavarth is marked as meaning and the four lines are natural. The three-step vidhi is attributed to tradition, there is a jaykara and a soft CTA, no date is given (panchang rule) and there are 3 tags. Nits: 'safed phool ... bhog lagayein' should be 'phool arpit karein, ghee ka bhog'. 'Bio mein link' only works on Instagram, so the WhatsApp version needs its own CTA line.

cards.name: Direct mail package (letter, postcard, self-mailer)
cards.summary: A printed mailing that has to survive the walk from letterbox to bin: an envelope teaser or postcard face that gets it opened or read, a letter that sells one offer to one reader, and a reply device that makes responding easy. Good packages read like a personal letter, are specific, and have a single response path.
use_for: Bank, NBFC or insurer cross-sell and renewal mailers
B2B mailers to CFOs, doctors or clinic owners with an invitation or sample
Donor and alumni appeal letters for an NGO or school
Real-estate or local-service postcards to a housing society
'Lumpy' mail with an object inside for account-based marketing
avoid: Writing it like a brochure, all features and no letter voice: write from one named person to one reader.
Several offers or ways to respond: one offer, one real deadline, one response path (call, QR, reply card).
Cheap one-time offers to a cold postal list in India, where good lists are thin: test WhatsApp (genre:whatsapp_broadcast) or email first.
Envelopes or notices styled like a government, court or bank-official letter: misleading, and against the ASCI code.

cards.goal: Respond through the one response path (call, scan the QR, return the reply card) before the deadline.

structure.does: A teaser line that earns the open, or a plain personal-looking envelope for a letter meant to feel personal. A postcard face carries headline, image and offer, readable at a glance.
Salutation by name where the data allows; the first lines speak to the reader's situation or make a specific promise, never the company history.
Develops the one offer: the problem, what is offered, proof (named client, number, testimonial), price, why now. Short paragraphs; subheads in long letters.
Exact offer, a real deadline date, how to respond (phone, QR with short URL, reply card) and what happens next.
A real, named person with a title.
Restates the main benefit and the deadline for readers who skim to the end.
Pre-filled name and address, tick-box choices, the offer restated, QR code and short URL, return instructions; works even if separated from the letter.

length.note: Postcards run 40-120 words; a one-page letter 300-500; long letters for considered purchases or donations run several pages. The price and unfamiliarity of the offer drive length.

checklist: Is there exactly one offer and one primary response path?
Does the letter's first line talk about the reader's situation or the offer, not the company?
Is the deadline a real date rather than 'hurry'?
Is there at least one specific proof point (named customer, number or guarantee)?
Is the letter signed by a named person with a title?
Does a P.S. restate the offer or the deadline?
Does the reply device repeat the offer and work on its own if separated?
Is all online response given as a QR code or short URL, with no 'click' language in print?
Are personalisation fields marked ([First name]) with a stated fallback?
Is nothing on the envelope or postcard styled like a government or legal notice?
pitfalls: Company-first openings ('Founded in 1998, XYZ...'): rewrite the first line around the reader's problem or the offer.
Merge-field disasters ('Dear [FNAME]', wrong gender, wrong title): specify a fallback for every field in the copy deck ('Dear Dr Sharma' falls back to 'Dear Doctor').
A postcard carrying a paragraph on the front: the face gets a glance, so put headline, offer and response there and detail on the back.
No way to measure response: give each mailing its own phone extension, short URL or QR so the client can count replies.
Translated English letters for Hindi or Marathi readers: transcreate the greeting and the proof (local names, local places), not just the words.
cards.exemplar_brief: One-page direct-mail letter plus reply card from a Pune physiotherapy clinic chain to residents aged 50+ in nearby housing societies, offering a free knee-and-back screening this month with a named senior physiotherapist; English with a one-line Marathi greeting allowed; letter 300-450 words + reply card 40-60 words; goal: call or scan the QR to book a slot before the stated date.

verified.note: Reader-first opening about stairs and puja-sitting pain; one offer, phone as the primary path with QR as backup, real dates whose weekdays are right (Mon 19, Sat 24, Sat 31 Oct 2026), a named physio placeholder with title, a P.S. restating offer and deadline, and a reply card that works on its own. Merge field has a Marathi fallback. Nits: the envelope is called 'plain' but carries a teaser. No per-mailing extension or short URL for response tracking.

cards.name: Display / banner ad copy
cards.summary: Copy for fixed-size or responsive display ads: a headline, an optional sub-line and a button, read at a glance beside unrelated content. Good banner copy names one benefit or offer, adds what the image cannot show, makes the click obvious, and fits every asset limit of the ad network.
use_for: Google responsive display ad assets (short headlines, long headline, descriptions)
Retargeting banners for an e-commerce sale
Standard banner-size sets for a launch (rectangle, leaderboard, mobile banner)
App-install and lead-generation display ads
avoid: A paragraph on a banner: if it needs explaining, it belongs on the landing page (genre:landing_page).
Words that repeat the image ('Shoes' over a picture of shoes): let the words carry the offer, proof or benefit.
Unproven superlatives ('India's No.1'): ASCI requires substantiation and a banner has no room for it; use a specific fact you can prove.
Fake system-alert or close-button styling ('Your phone has a virus'): deceptive, and rejected by networks (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation).

cards.goal: Click through to the landing page, or at least register the brand and offer, from a single glance.

structure.does: The one benefit or offer in plain words, key word first because small sizes and responsive layouts truncate.
structure.length: 2-6 words, within the network's character limit

structure.does: Proof, qualifier or detail: price, deadline, who it is for. Dropped on the smallest sizes.
Verb + object that matches what the landing page lets the user do ('Shop the sale', 'Get your quote').
Brand name and any mandatory disclaimer ('T&C apply', financial-product warnings), legible at the smallest size.
For responsive ads, 3-5 headlines and descriptions on different angles (offer, benefit, proof, deadline); each must make sense combined with any other because the network mixes them.

length.note: One banner is 5-20 words; a responsive asset set with variants runs 60-120. The network's character limits (plat:google_ads_responsive_display) and the smallest size in the set decide it.

checklist: Does each headline make sense on its own and when paired with any description?
Is every asset within the network's character limit?
Is the offer or key word in the first three words?
Is there exactly one CTA, phrased as a verb?
Does the CTA match what the landing page actually lets the user do?
Is every claim (price, % off, ranking) true and provable?
Do the words add something the image doesn't already show?
Does the smallest size still carry headline + CTA without the sub-line?
Is any mandatory disclaimer included?
pitfalls: One copy for every size: a leaderboard and a mobile banner need different cuts. Write the smallest version first, then expand.
Combinable assets that clash: responsive ads mix headlines and descriptions, so 'Sale ends Sunday' next to 'New arrivals every day' reads oddly. Check each pairing.
Hard-coded prices that go stale after the sale: use the client's product feed or keep the price out.
Hinglish on a banner works for mass D2C ('Sale shuru, stock khatam hone se pehle') but keep the button in the language of the landing page.
Exclamation marks and capitals for energy: networks restrict gimmicky punctuation and capitals (comp:google_ads_editorial); let the offer do the work.
cards.exemplar_brief: Google responsive display asset set for a Jaipur block-print bedsheet D2C brand's Diwali sale (flat 30% off until a stated date), retargeting shoppers who abandoned a cart; English with one Hinglish variant; 5 short headlines, 1 long headline, 3 descriptions and a CTA, each within the limits in plat:google_ads_responsive_display; goal: return to the cart and buy.

verified.note: All assets are within RDA limits. The offer is in the first words, the angles differ (offer, cart reminder, origin, deadline, Hinglish), the pairings combine cleanly, there is one verb CTA and a legal line. The 8 Nov end date matches Diwali 2026. Risk: description 2 says 'Your cart is saved at the sale price'. That claim about cart behaviour must be true on the client's store, or Google misrepresentation applies. The Hinglish headline would read more naturally as 'Jo cart mein hai, ab 30% off'.

cards.name: Documentary / long-form narration script
cards.summary: Narration written to picture after the paper edit: it gives the viewer what the footage and interviews cannot (time, place, context, stakes, transitions) and stays silent when pictures and voices carry the story. Good narration is written for the ear, says less than you expect, and never describes what is already on screen.
use_for: YouTube mini-documentaries on history, business or civic stories
Brand, CSR or NGO impact films
Archive-led explainer documentaries
Narrated segments inside a long-form channel episode
avoid: Narrating the image ('Here we see the river'): add what the picture cannot show (when, why it matters, what changed).
Wall-to-wall VO: leave room for interviews, natural sound and music; cut any line the edit already says.
Writing before the paper edit: you will write lines no shot supports. Wait for the selects, or mark the draft 'to be timed to picture'.
Opinion presented as fact in a factual documentary: attribute it, or move the piece to genre:video_essay_script.

cards.goal: Keep watching to the end, understanding what happened and why it matters.

structure.does: The strongest scene or interview bite first, then one narration line that states the film's question or stakes.
Place, time, who we follow and what is at stake: only the context the next scene needs.
Each act turns on a question; narration bridges scenes (time jumps, places, numbers), sets up interview bites and then gets out of their way.
structure.length: 2-5 acts; VO in short blocks between bites

structure.does: The moment of change, usually carried by interviews, archive and sound with minimal VO.
What changed and where things stand now, with dates; one reflective line, no moral lecture.
Current status, sources, disclaimers (reconstructions, AI-generated visuals) and credits.

length.note: VO words only. Narration covers part of the runtime, so a 5-minute mini-doc may need a few hundred words and a 20-minute film a couple of thousand; how much the interviews carry decides it. Time every block with a read-aloud against the cut.

checklist: Is the script in two columns (picture | sound/VO), with every VO line paired to a shot or sequence?
Does no line merely describe what is visible on screen?
Is every fact, number and date checkable against a listed source?
Can each sentence be said in one breath at speaking pace?
Are interview bites set up without the narration repeating them?
Does the cold open state the film's question within the first minute?
Are numbers written for the ear (rounded where precision doesn't matter)?
Are reconstructions, archive and AI-generated visuals labelled?
Does the ending say where things stand now rather than moralise?
pitfalls: Encyclopaedia voice with long subordinate clauses that trip the narrator: read every line aloud at pace and split anything you run out of breath on.
Telling the audience how to feel ('In a heartbreaking turn...'): let the bite or the image do it; narration supplies facts.
Hindi VO with translated-English syntax or heavy Sanskritised words: write spoken Hindi (lang:hindustani_everyday) and test it with the narrator or TTS.
Numbers in a row: one number per sentence, and put the key figure on screen as a text card.
Unlabelled AI reconstructions in a factual film: label them; India's 2026 IT Rules on synthetic content and YouTube's altered-content disclosure apply.

ban.label: narrating the picture or the video itself

cards.exemplar_brief: Two-column narration script (picture | VO) for a 5-minute YouTube mini-documentary by a Patna-based history channel on the 1934 Bihar earthquake and how Munger and Patna rebuilt, built from archive photos and two historian interviews; Hindi (Devanagari) for a human narrator; 450-650 words of VO; goal: viewers watch to the end and subscribe for the next episode.

verified.note: Facts check out: 15 Jan 1934 was a Monday, the epicentre was in Nepal near Everest at about M8, Munger and Muzaffarpur were worst hit, Rajendra Prasad was released on 17 Jan and set up the Bihar Central Relief Committee, Patna was capital of Bihar and Orissa from 1912, and the GSI 1939 memoir is real. The spoken Hindi is strong ('har naksha kisi ki zameen par khinchta hai'), the cold open poses the question, and bites are set up and then left alone. The end card labels the archive with no AI visuals. Deductions: rows are PICTURE/SOUND/VO stacks rather than a true two-column table, and the rebuild content (the film's core) waits entirely on interview placeholders. The Patna section repeats itself ('prashasan yahin se chalta tha' twice).

cards.name: Marketing ebook (gated content)
cards.summary: A designed, multi-chapter guide given free in exchange for an email or phone number, which teaches one problem well enough that the right reader trusts the brand and the wrong reader self-selects out. Good ones deliver a framework, checklist, benchmark or case the reader cannot get from a search result, and end in one clear next step.
use_for: B2B SaaS or fintech top-of-funnel guide ('GST e-invoicing playbook for mid-size manufacturers')
Consultancy, CA or law-firm credibility piece promoted through LinkedIn ads
Edtech or coaching guide that feeds a webinar
Benchmark report built on the client's own data
avoid: Rewriting the top search results into chapters: AI answers give that away free. Add first-hand data, templates, cases or the client's own method.
A one-page checklist dressed up as an ebook: if one page does the job, write genre:lead_magnet_content.
A product brochure behind a form: readers who feel tricked unsubscribe. Teach first; sell in the last chapter.
Asking for more fields than needed or skipping consent wording: under DPDP, say what you will send and collect only what you need.

cards.goal: Hand over their email for it, read past chapter one, and take the one next step (book a call, start a trial, join the webinar).

structure.does: A specific outcome for a specific reader ('The GST Notice Playbook: the 6 notice types D2C founders get and how to answer each').
structure.length: title up to 10 words; subtitle up to 20

structure.does: The problem in the reader's words, who it is for and not for, what they will be able to do by the end, and why the author is credible (first-hand cases, numbers).
One idea or step per chapter, each with something the reader can apply: framework, worked example, checklist, template, Indian case. Descriptive subheads and callouts for skimmers.
Recap or checklist the reader can print or screenshot.
Bridges from what they learned to the product or service, with one CTA and one proof point.
Author or firm credentials, contact, and a reference for every statistic.

length.note: Working range; topic depth and funnel stage decide. Under about 1,500 words it is a checklist or guide, not an ebook. Usually commissioned with its landing page and a short delivery email sequence.

checklist: Does the title promise a specific outcome for a specific reader?
Does the introduction say who it is for and what they will be able to do after reading?
Does every chapter contain at least one usable artefact (framework, checklist, template or worked example)?
Is there first-hand material (client data, a real case, the author's process) a search result would not give?
Does every statistic carry a named source and year?
Do the subheads alone give the reader the argument?
Is selling confined to the final chapter, with one CTA?
Is there a one-page summary or checklist?
For Indian readers, are amounts in Rs with lakh/crore formatting and examples set in India?
pitfalls: Padding chapters ('What is GST?') the target reader doesn't need: start where their problem starts.
Stat soup from unsourced 'studies': every number gets a source and year, or it goes.
A pitch in every chapter: at most one soft mention per chapter; the CTA lives at the end.
A wall of text handed to the designer: mark callouts, tables and checklists in the copy deck so layout can follow the argument.
A gated asset with no follow-up: write the delivery and nurture emails with it (genre:email_sequence_nurture).
cards.exemplar_brief: Gated ebook for a Jaipur CA firm: 'GST notices for D2C founders: 6 common notice types and how to respond to each', for founders of D2C brands doing Rs 5-50 crore revenue; English; 3,000-3,800 words across an introduction, 6 short chapters, a one-page checklist and a CTA chapter; goal: book a 20-minute GST health-check call.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Now complete at 3,119 words: a real-reader intro that says who it is not for, six chapters in one repeatable shape each with an artefact (reconciliation sheet, monthly three-way check, missing-returns tracker, 7-working-day plan, refund reply pack, DRC-06 skeleton), a one-page triage table plus 10 checks, one CTA chapter. cards.name: Editorial (publication's institutional opinion)
cards.summary: An unsigned argument that states a publication's or board's official position on one issue and asks someone (government, regulator, public) to act. Good editorials take a clear side early, rest it on verified facts, deal fairly with the strongest counter-argument, and end with a specific demand rather than a vague hope.
use_for: A newspaper or digital outlet's lead editorial on a policy or event
An association's or institution's official position in its journal or newsletter
A trade magazine's editor-page lead on a new regulation
Campus newspaper editorial-board pieces
avoid: Writing in the first person or telling a personal story: that is a signed column (genre:opinion_column).
Fence-sitting ('only time will tell'): an editorial must say what should happen.
Re-reporting the news at length: summarise the peg in a sentence or two and argue.
Attacking a person's character, religion or caste: argue the policy (comp:bns_defamation_speech).

sources.title: Jasmine Roberts, Introduction to Journalism I (NVCC Pressbooks, CC BY-NC 4.0, 2023): Types of news stories

sources.title: EFA 2026 Rate Chart (2026-03-18)

buyers: Newspapers and digital news outlets (edit-page desks)

cards.goal: Accept the board's position and support or demand the specific action it calls for.

structure.does: States the position or the demand, not just the topic ('Desilt Patna's drains before the monsoon, not after').
One or two sentences on what prompted the editorial, then the board's stance, both in the first paragraph.
Two or three reasons, each resting on a verified fact, figure or precedent; strongest first.
The best opposing case stated fairly, then answered.
Who must do what, by when if possible; a final line that restates the position crisply.

length.note: The edit-page slot fixes the length; a lead editorial is usually the longest on the page and digital editorials often run shorter. Ask the desk for the slot.

checklist: Is the board's position stated in the first paragraph?
Is the piece free of first-person singular ('I', 'my', 'मैं')?
Does each argument rest on a fact, figure or precedent checked against its primary source?
Is the strongest counter-argument stated fairly and answered?
Does the close name who should do what (and by when, where possible)?
Is the news peg summarised in two sentences or fewer?
Is there no attack on anyone's identity, religion or caste?
Does the headline state the position rather than the topic?
pitfalls: A hedged conclusion ('Both sides have merit'): pick one and say why.
A strawman counter-argument: readers who hold that view stop reading. State it at its strongest.
Figures from memory: check every number against the budget document, court order or official dataset before filing.
For Hindi papers, ornate or calqued Hindi ('इस बात को सुनिश्चित किया जाना चाहिए'): write the argument in clean standard Hindi with short sentences and active verbs.

cards.exemplar_brief: Lead editorial for a Patna-based Hindi digital news outlet arguing that the city's municipal corporation should publish ward-wise drain-desilting progress before the monsoon; general readers in Patna; Hindi (Devanagari); 450-600 words; goal: readers back the demand and share the piece.

verified.note: Position-as-headline, peg plus stance in paragraph one, then three reasons, strongest first: 2019 waterlogging, public money with RTI s.4 proactive disclosure, and ward-level scrutiny. The counter-argument (exposure of shortfalls, paper inflation) is stated fairly and answered with verifiable data. The close names who (commissioner and mayor), what (a ward table with contractor and spend) and when (7 days, then every Friday until the monsoon). Clean standard Hindi with local 'udahi'; no first person singular. Public facts used are correct: 75 wards, the Sept 2019 flooding, a mid-June monsoon. Peg date left as a placeholder by design.

cards.name: Editorial email newsletter
cards.summary: A recurring email issue readers open for the writing itself: an essay, analysis or annotated roundup in a consistent voice and format. Good issues deliver one clear idea (or a tightly edited set of items) per send, carry a subject line that earns the open honestly, and follow a structure readers learn to trust.
use_for: A founder's or company's weekly insight newsletter (Substack, beehiiv, LinkedIn newsletter)
A media brand's daily or weekly analysis email
An expert's paid newsletter
A B2B industry briefing that keeps a brand in the inbox
avoid: Using it as a promo blast: offers and launches go to genre:promotional_email; the newsletter stays value-first with at most one labelled sponsor or house-ad block.
Pasting a blog post with 'read more' links: write for the inbox so the email is complete on its own.
Link dumps without a take: if curation is the product, write genre:curated_newsletter.
Changing the format every issue: readers come back for a known shape.

cards.goal: Open it, read to the end, and come back next issue (reply, forward, or click the one featured link).

structure.does: The subject names the issue's idea specifically; the preheader adds a second reason to open; the sender name never changes.
Gets straight into the idea with a scene, a number or a question; no 'Welcome to issue 47'.
One idea developed with evidence and the writer's view; subheads once it passes about 600 words.
Fixed blocks readers expect: three links with one-line takes, a reader question, a chart of the week.
One clearly labelled block, written in the newsletter's voice.
Personal sign-off and one ask: reply, forward, share or upgrade.

length.note: Daily briefs sit at the low end, weekly essays at 800-2,000 words. Keep the HTML small enough to avoid Gmail clipping (plat:gmail_clipping).

checklist: Does the draft include a subject line and a preheader that don't repeat each other?
Does the first sentence start the idea instead of greeting or apologising?
Is there one main idea a reader could sum up in a sentence?
Does every claim or number link to its source?
Is any sponsored block labelled as sponsored?
Is link text descriptive (no 'click here')?
Is there exactly one primary ask at the end?
Does the issue follow the newsletter's fixed section format?
Would the email make sense to a reader who never clicks a link?
pitfalls: Throat-clearing intros ('Hope you had a great week!'): open with the idea.
Image-heavy templates that clip in Gmail or land in Promotions: keep it text-led with few images.
Subject lines the body doesn't pay off: a one-time open spike, then unsubscribes. The subject must describe the real content.
Hinglish creator newsletters: fine in Roman script if the voice is consistent, but keep subject lines in the script most of the list reads.
cards.exemplar_brief: Weekly issue of 'Paisa Pulse', the newsletter of a Mumbai fintech founder, explaining one idea: why zero-MDR UPI makes it hard for payment apps to earn from UPI payments, for startup operators and finance-curious professionals; English with light Hinglish; 700-1,000 words plus subject line and preheader; goal: read to the end and reply with a question.

verified.note: Subject and preheader do different jobs. It opens on a chai-stall scene with no greeting, keeps one idea (who pays for zero-MDR UPI), clearly labels the illustration, gives a candid 'My view', fixed 'three reads' links and a single reply ask. The Hinglish is light and natural. Fact precision: s.10A came in via the Finance (No. 2) Act 2019. The PPI wallet interchange is 0.5-1.1 percent by merchant category, so 1.1 percent is the ceiling, not a flat fee (writer did flag [verify]). One read link is a pure placeholder.

cards.name: E-learning course / training module script
cards.summary: The script and storyboard for one training module: measurable objectives, short screens or scenes that each teach one point, narration written for the ear, on-screen text that supports rather than repeats it, and knowledge checks tied to each objective. Good modules change what the learner does on the job, not just what they have seen.
use_for: Corporate compliance and soft-skills modules (POSH awareness, data privacy, customer handling)
Product training for channel partners and field sales
LMS onboarding modules
Government or NGO training for frontline workers, often in Hindi
Narrated slide-based or AI-avatar video lessons
avoid: Starting from content ('everything about our product'): write 3-5 'learner will be able to...' objectives first and cut anything that serves none of them.
Narration that reads the screen text aloud: the screen carries keywords and visuals, the VO explains.
Quizzes that test trivia ('In which year was the policy introduced?'): test decisions in a realistic scenario.
A single lesson for a public creator course: use genre:course_lesson_script.

cards.goal: Do the target task correctly on the job, with the module's assessment as the proof.

structure.does: Title, audience, duration and 3-5 measurable objectives using observable verbs (identify, calculate, choose, respond).
A realistic workplace situation or consequence the learner recognises.
One concept per screen or scene, in storyboard columns: screen no. | visual and on-screen text | narration | interaction | developer notes. Each chunk maps to an objective.
The learner applies the concept: branching choice or case, with feedback for every option.
Questions mapped to objectives, plausible distractors based on real mistakes, and feedback explaining why for right and wrong answers.
Key takeaways, a downloadable checklist, and where to get help.

length.note: Screen count and narration drive length; microlearning stays to a few minutes, full modules run longer. Agree the module duration first and budget narration words from a timed read-aloud.

checklist: Are there 3-5 objectives, each with an observable verb (not 'understand' or 'know')?
Does every screen map to at least one objective?
Does every objective have at least one knowledge-check question?
Does narration differ from on-screen text (VO explains, screen shows keywords)?
Does every quiz option have feedback explaining why it is right or wrong?
Are scenarios set in the learner's real workplace, with Indian names, roles and tools where relevant?
Can each narration block be read aloud naturally in one take?
Could a developer build each screen from the storyboard without guessing (visual, interaction, branching)?
Is there a summary or job aid at the end?
pitfalls: 'Understand the policy' objectives that cannot be tested: rewrite as 'choose the correct escalation path for a customer complaint'.
Screens copied from the policy PDF: keep the screen to keywords and a visual, and move detail to the job aid.
Obviously wrong distractors: write wrong options that reflect mistakes people actually make.
Hindi modules translated word for word from English: transcreate scenarios and examples (lang:transcreation), and keep technical terms in the form learners actually say.
No feedback on wrong answers: 'Incorrect, try again' teaches nothing; explain the consequence of that choice.

cards.exemplar_brief: Script + storyboard for one 10-minute e-learning module for a Lucknow-based NBFC's new loan-collection agents: 'Calling a borrower who has missed an EMI: respectful, compliant collection calls'; 3-4 objectives, 8-10 screens with narration, one branching call scenario, 4 knowledge-check questions with feedback; Hindi (Devanagari) narration with English UI labels; 900-1,400 words; goal: agents choose compliant, respectful responses in the scenario.

verified.note: Developer-ready storyboard: 4 observable objectives, a realistic Aminabad hook, 10 screens each mapped to objectives, and a two-part branching call with feedback on every option. The job aid and grievance route are present, and the 8am-7pm window matches RBI's recovery-agent directions. Deductions: Q2 is labelled objective 2 but tests objective 1 (third party picks up), so objective 2 ('paise nahi hain' response) has no knowledge-check question. Objectives are phrased as commands ('bataen') after 'kar payenge'. Option B line 'Bete ki sehat ke liye dua. Aap seedha bataiye' is clunky and a little brusque for the respectful model answer.

cards.name: Election manifesto
cards.summary: A party's or candidate's published promises for an election, organised by sector or voter group, each specific enough to be checked later and, per ECI guidelines, accompanied by its rationale and a broad indication of how it will be funded. Good manifestos are readable by ordinary voters, consistent with the Constitution, and distil into a few headline promises for posters and speeches.
use_for: A party's sankalp patra or ghoshna patra for a state or national election
An independent candidate's constituency manifesto
Municipal or panchayat election vision documents
Student-union or professional-body election manifestos
Summary versions: a 10-point leaflet, a WhatsApp card series, speech talking points
avoid: Vague promises ('we will develop the state'): name the measure, the number and the deadline.
Costly promises with no funding logic: ECI guidelines ask manifestos to broadly indicate the ways and means; add a funding line per costly promise.
Appeals to caste or communal feeling, or anything repugnant to the Constitution: the MCC prohibits it; argue on policy.
Releasing in the prohibitory period before polling: check the ECI compendium and the client's legal cell.

sources.title: ECI Compendium of Instructions on Model Code of Conduct (hosted by CEO Bihar)
sources.supports: Part VIII manifesto guidelines (ECI letter 437/6/Manifesto/2013, 19.02.2014): nothing repugnant to the Constitution; manifesto should reflect the rationale for promises and broadly indicate the ways and means to meet the financial requirement; MCC general conduct on criticism of other parties

sources.title: EFA 2026 Rate Chart (2026-03-18)
sources.supports: Other Consulting (grant writing, pitch development, proposal development, strategic communications): $87.50-135.00 per hour

buyers: Party manifesto committees and research cells
Student and professional bodies holding elections
cards.value_why: Every party issues one per election and ECI regulates its content (MCC Part VIII). Drafting runs through party committees and political consultancies on campaign retainers, not open marketplaces; the EFA 2026 strategic-communications consulting rate ($87.50-135/hr) is the nearest priced benchmark.
cards.goal: Believe the party or candidate has a credible plan for their concerns, remember a few headline promises, and vote for it.

structure.does: Name of the document, party or candidate, election and year, and a one-line vision.
A signed message: the moment, the vision, the commitment to voters. Short and personal.
The 5-10 flagship promises on one page, one line each, specific and countable.
Per sector or voter group (farmers, youth, women, health, infrastructure): the current situation in one paragraph, then numbered promises; each costly promise with its rationale and funding route.
Incumbent: delivery figures with official sources. Challenger: factual gaps in the record. Policy only, never private lives.
Timelines, the mechanism that will deliver, and the broad fiscal plan.
Restates the vision and asks for the vote.

length.note: Full state or national manifestos run long; constituency manifestos and summary leaflets are short. Writers draft chapter by chapter, so a single draft is usually one chapter or the headline page.

checklist: Is every promise specific enough to verify later (number, scope, deadline)?
Does each costly promise state its rationale and a funding route?
Is there no appeal on the basis of caste, religion or community?
Is each promise within the powers of the body being elected (a municipal manifesto doesn't promise central schemes)?
Are record or performance claims sourced to official data?
Is criticism of opponents limited to their policies, programmes and record?
Is there a one-page list of headline promises that stands alone?
Is it written in the voters' language and register, with each scheme explained in one line?
Are AI-generated images or synthetic content labelled as ECI directions require?
pitfalls: Copy-paste from the last manifesto: journalists and opponents compare versions. Update the data and drop delivered or dead promises.
Numbers that don't add up: a promise costing more than the relevant budget head invites ridicule. Ask the policy cell to cost every flagship promise.
Bureaucratic Hindi ('सुनिश्चित किया जाएगा' in every line): vary the verbs, write the way leaders speak, keep sentences short.
Personal attacks on rival leaders: the MCC confines criticism to policies, programmes and past record.
cards.exemplar_brief: Youth-employment chapter of a fictional regional party's 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly election sankalp patra: a one-paragraph situation summary, 6-8 numbered promises with rationale and a funding route for each costly one, and a one-line headline promise for the cover page; Hindi (Devanagari); 700-1,100 words; goal: a first-time voter finds the plan specific and credible.

verified.note: Situation in one paragraph naming three problems; seven numbered promises, each with deadline or scope, a 'kyon' and a 'kharch' line. The arithmetic reconciles (3,600 + 900 + 150 + 300 = 4,950 crore), FRBM is respected, every promise sits within state powers, there are no caste or religion appeals, and the Hindi is direct rather than bureaucratic. Deduction: the cover-page line ('samay par bharti, samay par natije, kaam milne tak sahara') is a slogan, not the specific, countable headline promise the card asks for (e.g. '10 lakh yuvaon ko Rs 3,000 bhatta, 12 mahine mein bharti').

cards.name: Elevator pitch / boilerplate description
cards.summary: A few sentences that say who the company helps, with what, and why it is different, written to be said aloud in an intro or pasted as a press boilerplate and profile description. Good ones use the customer's words, carry one concrete proof point and no category buzzwords, and come as a matched set (one line, 30 seconds spoken, ~100-word boilerplate) that all say the same thing.
use_for: Press-release 'About' boilerplate
Founder's spoken intro at events, investor meetings and podcasts
LinkedIn company About, Google Business Profile and directory descriptions
Company overview in tenders and RFP responses
Sales team's one-line intro for calls and emails
avoid: Buzzword stacks ('AI-powered end-to-end innovative solutions provider'): say what you do in words a customer would use.
Different versions saying different things across channels: write one master set and derive every profile from it.
Pasting the internal positioning statement as public copy: build from genre:positioning_statement, but in plain, speakable language.
Personal career intros: use genre:professional_bio or genre:personal_brand_statement.

cards.goal: Understand in one hearing what the company does and for whom, then ask a follow-up question or remember it well enough to refer someone.

structure.does: The specific customer and their situation ('D2C brands doing Rs 5-50 crore a year').
The problem solved or outcome, in the customer's words, not a feature list.
The mechanism or difference a competitor could not claim in the same words.
One concrete number, named client or credential.
Spoken: an invitation to continue ('Who handles GST notices at your brand?'). Boilerplate: founded year, HQ, scale, website, media contact.

checklist: Does it name a specific customer group?
Does it state the outcome in words a customer would use?
Is there at least one concrete proof point (number, named client or credential)?
Is it free of stacked buzzwords ('innovative', 'cutting-edge', 'one-stop', 'end-to-end')?
Can the spoken version be said aloud in about 30 seconds without running out of breath?
Do the one-liner, spoken and boilerplate versions say the same thing?
Does the boilerplate carry the facts a journalist needs (founded, HQ, scale, website)?
Is every superlative ('largest', 'first') substantiated or removed?
pitfalls: Category-first openings ('We are a leading SaaS platform...'): start with the customer and the problem.
Too many audiences in one line: write for the primary customer and make separate variants for investors or recruits.
Spoken Hindi or Hinglish versions translated literally: rewrite them the way the founder actually talks in that room.
Stale numbers in boilerplates: date every figure and review the set each quarter.
AI assistants and journalists quote boilerplates verbatim (trend:geo_ai_search): make the first sentence a self-contained factual definition of what the company is.
cards.exemplar_brief: Messaging set for a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C founders doing Rs 5-50 crore revenue: a one-line description (up to 20 words), a 30-second spoken intro for a founders' meetup, and a press-release boilerplate of 80-110 words; English; goal: a founder hearing it asks 'how does that work?'.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. The D2C mechanism (rebuilding the month from marketplace payout reports, returns and cancelled COD parcels) now runs through all three versions, so they say the same thing; the spoken intro opens on a question every founder recognises ('a sales figure you did not recognise'), runs about 80 words and closes on a conversation question; the boilerplate is 85 words with a self-contained first sentence and journalist slots. Proof is a slot because the brief gives none. Nit (writer): the one-liner switches from 'We' to 'your'. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Nurture / drip email sequence
cards.summary: A planned series of automated emails that moves a lead from first interest to a sales conversation or purchase over days or weeks. Good sequences are mapped before they are written: each email has one job, one CTA and a reason to exist at that point; timing, behaviour branches and exit rules are specified; and every email is worth reading even if the reader never buys.
use_for: Nurture after an ebook download or webinar for B2B leads
Free-trial-to-paid SaaS sequences beyond the welcome emails
Course or coaching pre-launch sequences
Long-cycle lead nurture for real estate or higher education
Re-engaging cold leads before list cleaning
avoid: Writing emails one at a time without a map: agree the sequence map (goal, trigger, delay, exit) first.
Every email a pitch: alternate value emails (case, how-to, objection answer) with asks.
No exit rules: people who buy or book must leave the sequence at once; 'Still thinking?' sent to a new customer loses trust.
The first emails right after sign-up are genre:welcome_email_series; cart recovery is genre:abandoned_cart_email.

buyers: B2B SaaS and services marketing teams
cards.value_why: Fiverr's Email Copy category filters 'Email Sequences', AWAI lists 'Autoresponder/Funnel Emails (Series)', and Upwork In-Demand Skills 2026 puts Email Marketing and Marketing Automation in the top-10 Sales & Marketing skills. Sold as a multi-email package, so it prices above single emails.
cards.goal: Take the sequence's one conversion action (book a call, start a paid plan, buy) when ready, and keep opening until then.

structure.does: A table agreed before any copy: email no., trigger and delay, job (deliver, teach, prove, answer objection, ask), subject, CTA, branch or exit rule.
Delivers what they signed up for, says what is coming and how often, asks for one small action (reply, save the sender).
Each teaches one thing tied to the buyer's problem (a how-to, a case, a myth busted) with a soft CTA.
A case study with numbers, a testimonial, and answers to the top one or two objections (price, time, trust).
The clear offer, a real reason or deadline for acting now, risk reversal, one CTA.
A short final note: deadline reminder or 'should I stop emailing about this?', then the lead moves to the regular newsletter.

length.note: Whole sequence, every email with subject, preheader, body and CTA. A short B2B nurture is a handful of emails; launch and long-cycle sequences run longer. The length of the buying decision sets the count and the gaps.

checklist: Is there a sequence map with trigger, delay, job, CTA and exit rule for every email?
Does each email have exactly one primary CTA?
Does every email have a subject line and a preheader?
Do at least half the emails give value without asking for the sale?
Is there an exit rule that removes people who convert?
Is every deadline or scarcity claim a real limit?
Does every email carry an unsubscribe line and identify the sender?
Does every personalisation token have a fallback?
Does each email make sense if it is the only one the reader opens?
Does the last email say what happens next (moved to the newsletter, or emails stop)?
pitfalls: The same shape every time (story then pitch): readers learn to skip. Vary it: a plain-text note, a case, an FAQ, a one-line question.
Fake urgency ('Only 3 seats left!' on an evergreen course): a dark pattern under the CCPA 2023 guidelines, and sequence readers see it repeat.
Spacing that ignores the buying cycle: a flat buyer deciding over months does not need daily email. Space by decision length.
Heavy HTML templates with many links and images: a plain-text style reads as personal and is kinder to deliverability (trend:email_deliverability_rules).
Pasting the same copy into WhatsApp: WhatsApp needs opt-in, an approved template and a shorter conversational version (genre:whatsapp_broadcast).
cards.exemplar_brief: 5-email nurture sequence for a Jaipur CA firm, sent over 14 days to D2C founders (Rs 5-50 crore revenue) who downloaded its GST-notice ebook: a sequence map table, then each email with subject, preheader, body, one CTA and an unsubscribe line, ending with an invitation to a free 20-minute GST health check; English; 900-1,400 words in total; goal: book the call.

verified.note: Full map with send day, job, subject, CTA and exit; every email has subject, preheader, one CTA, sender, unsubscribe and a token fallback. Shapes vary (deliver/ask reply, a 10-minute check, a case, an objection, an offer), the 'already have an accountant' objection is handled well, and the 20th GSTR-3B date for monthly filers is real urgency, not fake. The last email says what happens next. Nits: email 3 rests entirely on a client case placeholder (by design), and 'the notice was rarely about money owed' generalises from one case. Email 2 omits that DRC-01B/01C only trigger above the notified threshold.

cards.name: Error message copy
cards.summary: Short interface messages that say what went wrong, why if it helps, and exactly how to fix it, shown next to the problem in plain words without blaming the user. Good error copy keeps the user's input and gets them moving again; a message that only says something failed is a dead end.
use_for: Form validation (sign-up, KYC, checkout)
Payment failures and UPI timeouts
Network, server and 404 states
API and CLI error strings developers read
Permission-denied and no-results states
avoid: Codes and jargon ('Error 0x80070005', 'Invalid input'): say what is wrong in the user's terms and show the fix; put the code in a secondary line for support.
Blame ('You entered an invalid PAN'): describe the requirement neutrally ('PAN has 10 characters, like ABCDE1234F').
Jokes on serious failures (money debited, order not placed): be calm, say whether they were charged and what happens next.
Errors shown while the user is still typing: validate when they leave the field or submit.

cards.goal: Understand what went wrong and fix it, or know what happens next, without contacting support or abandoning the task.

structure.does: Where the message appears: next to the field or element that caused it; page-level errors at the top with links to each field.
The problem in the user's terms.
Only when it helps fix it or reassures ('Your bank didn't respond in time').

structure.part: How to fix or what happens next
structure.does: The specific action, with the expected format or an example; or what the system is doing and when (refund timing).
Button or link that performs the fix ('Try again', 'Use another UPI ID'), with the user's input kept.
Error code or reference ID in secondary text for support.

length.note: One inline message is roughly 5-25 words; a draft usually covers the set of states for one flow, which is where the upper bound comes from. A bilingual EN+HI set doubles the count: about 500-650 words for 8-10 states.

checklist: Does each message say what went wrong in the user's terms, with no raw code or bare 'invalid input'?
Does each message say how to fix it or what happens next?
Is every message free of blame words ('invalid', 'illegal', 'you failed')?
Does every format error show the expected format or an example?
Is each action button a specific verb?
For money errors, does it say whether the user was charged and when any refund arrives?
Is each message readable in one glance (one or two short sentences)?
Are exclamation marks and jokes absent?
Is terminology identical to the rest of the UI ('UPI ID' everywhere, not 'VPA' in one place)?
Is the error stated in text, not only by red colour or an icon?
pitfalls: A single 'Something went wrong' for everything: list the top failure causes with engineering and write a specific message for each; keep the generic one as a last resort with retry and a support route.
Forms that clear on error: ask engineering to keep the input; no copy can make up for retyping.
Word-for-word Hindi ('अमान्य इनपुट') that nobody understands: write what to do ('मोबाइल नंबर 10 अंकों का होना चाहिए').
Over-apologising or cute copy on a failed payment: people worry about money; be direct and specific.
Messages that expose internals (stack traces, table names): a security risk. Log the detail and show a reference ID.
cards.exemplar_brief: Error-message set for a Bengaluru UPI payments app's 'Send money' flow: 8-10 states (wrong UPI ID format, UPI ID not found, insufficient balance, bank server down, payment timed out with money debited, daily limit reached, wrong UPI PIN, no internet), each with message, action button and helper text, in English and Hindi (Devanagari); under 25 words per message; goal: the user fixes the problem or knows exactly when their money comes back.

verified.note: 8 states, each with what happened, the fix or next step, a specific verb button and helper text, and input kept. Money states say whether the user was charged; the timeout state says 'Don't pay again' with a reversal date, consistent with RBI's T+1 rule for failed UPI debits. No blame words, and the Hindi is natural ('bhugtan atka hai'). Nits: EN uses 'Rs' while HI uses the rupee sign; '{n} tries' needs a singular form; 'add money first' is wallet wording for a bank account. The max_words fail is the card's fault, not the piece's. cards.name: ESG / CSR / sustainability report copy
cards.summary: Narrative and disclosure copy for sustainability, CSR and BRSR reports: the leadership letter, materiality and strategy narrative, pillar chapters, programme stories and the text around data tables. Good ESG copy ties every claim to a figure, baseline, boundary and period, reports setbacks alongside wins, and never lets a green adjective stand in for data.
use_for: BRSR narrative sections in a listed company's annual report
Standalone sustainability or ESG reports
CSR annual reports and programme impact stories
Corporate foundation and NGO impact reports
ESG pages on a corporate website
avoid: Unquantified green claims ('eco-friendly', 'sustainable', 'carbon neutral'): give the metric, scope, baseline and verification, or drop the claim.
Reporting only wins: missed targets and material risks stated plainly build credibility; omissions read as greenwashing.
Brochure tone in a disclosure document: factual, measured prose; keep storytelling for the impact case studies.
Producing or estimating disclosure numbers: the writer narrates data supplied and signed off by the sustainability and finance teams.

sources.title: Upwork: hire Sustainability Freelancers
sources.supports: ESG/CSR report writing (GRI, SASB) listed among sustainability freelance services (snippet-only)

The EFA 2026 business/marketing ghostwriting rate (50 cents-$1 per word) is the nearest price benchmark.
cards.goal: Trust that the company's sustainability claims are real and material, and (for investors and raters) find each disclosure with its data.

structure.does: The year's ESG priorities, progress against stated targets with numbers, one honest setback, commitments ahead.
Reporting period, boundary (which entities and sites), frameworks used, assurance status, contact.
Material topics, how they were identified (stakeholder engagement), and why each matters to the business.
Per topic: policy, target, performance with year-on-year data against the baseline, actions taken, what is next. Tables carry the numbers; prose explains them.
Specific programmes: place, beneficiaries, spend, measured outcome, and a short beneficiary story used with consent.
Labels, footnotes and framework index wording around the client's tables.

length.note: A BRSR narrative section or CSR chapter runs a few thousand words; standalone sustainability reports run far longer. Writers deliver chapter by chapter, and the data tables come from the client.

checklist: Does every environmental or social claim carry a number, unit, period and boundary?
Are year-on-year comparisons made against a stated baseline year?
Are missed targets and negative trends reported rather than omitted?
Is every figure traceable to the client's signed-off data table?
Are words like 'green', 'eco-friendly', 'sustainable' and 'net zero' either defined with data and scope or removed?
Are the reporting boundary and framework stated?
Are beneficiary stories specific (place, programme, outcome) and used with consent?
Is the assurance status stated accurately?
Is technical terminology (for example Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions) used consistently and correctly?
pitfalls: Greenwashing by adjective ('our eco-friendly packaging'): replace with the measured fact and its scope and period, or cut it.
Net-zero or 'carbon neutral' claims without the pathway: state the target year, the scopes covered and the role of offsets, or don't make the claim.
Cherry-picked baselines that flatter the trend: use the baseline the company committed to, and explain any change.
CSR as photo-op: listing spend and events without outcomes. Report what changed for beneficiaries and how it was measured.
Hindi or regional summaries for local stakeholders: translate the facts precisely and add no promotional flourish missing from the English.
cards.exemplar_brief: Environment chapter narrative for the BRSR section of a fictional mid-cap Gujarat textile manufacturer's annual report: energy, water and waste performance against an FY2022-23 baseline, using an illustrative data table the writer includes and labels as sample data, one missed water target explained, and next year's targets; English for investors and ESG raters; 900-1,300 words; goal: a rater finds every claim backed by a figure, period and boundary.

verified.note: Rater-ready. Period, baseline (FY2022-23, not restated), boundary (3 units plus office, Scope 3 excluded), framework (BRSR P6) and assurance slot are all stated. The sample table is internally consistent: I recomputed every intensity and percentage change and the target arithmetic. The missed water target is explained with a gap of about 76 ML, matching 62 + 13. The negative is reported plainly and the target carried forward, not reset, with owners. No green adjectives. Nit: voice switches between 'the Company' and 'we'.

cards.name: Eulogy
cards.summary: A short spoken tribute at a funeral, memorial or shraddhanjali sabha that honours one life through specific memories rather than adjectives. Good eulogies are personal, exact about names and relationships, allow one moment of warmth or gentle humour, and end with what the person leaves behind.
use_for: A family member's tribute at a funeral or shraddhanjali sabha
A colleague's or company's tribute at a condolence meeting
A tribute to a community, school or institution leader
A written version for a memorial booklet or social post
avoid: A chronological CV ('born in 1948, joined the bank in 1971...'): choose three stories that show who they were.
Settling scores or airing family conflict: the room is grieving; keep to what honours the person.
Inside jokes the room can't follow: explain in one line or pick another story.
A published death report or notice: use genre:obituary or genre:obituary_notice; a note to the family is genre:condolence_message.

sources.title: Fiverr Writing & Translation: Speechwriting
sources.supports: personal speeches sold under speechwriting

buyers: Families, directly or through a speechwriter
Companies and institutions holding condolence meetings
cards.value_why: Occasional one-off commissions sold under speechwriting (Fiverr Speechwriting); most eulogies are written by family members.
cards.goal: Feel the person's presence in the room for a few minutes and leave with a memory of who they were.

structure.does: Who the speaker is and their relationship to the person; one line on what they want to share.
A defining trait shown through one specific story (a place, an action, words they used).
Specific moments, each showing a different side of the person; one may carry gentle humour.
What family, colleagues or the community carry forward; their values seen in action.
A goodbye to them or to the room; a line, prayer or saying they loved; thanks for coming if the speaker is family.

length.note: Read it aloud with a timer: organisers usually give each speaker a few minutes, and grief slows delivery. More speakers means shorter.

checklist: Are names, dates, relationships and places confirmed with the family?
Are there at least two specific stories (place, action or words), not just adjectives?
Does the speaker say who they are and how they knew the person?
Is there nothing that embarrasses the family or airs a dispute?
Does any humour come from affection for the person, at no one's expense?
Does it end with what the person leaves behind or a farewell?
Does a read-aloud fit the time the organisers gave?
Is it written in the speaker's own voice and language mix?
Are religious references (prayer, shloka, verse) right for the family's faith and tradition?
pitfalls: Adjective lists ('kind, generous, hardworking'): turn each into a moment. 'Every Sunday he took the 7 a.m. bus to teach maths at the village school' says generous better.
A register the speaker never uses: if they speak Hindi-English mix at home, the eulogy should too; stiff formal Hindi sounds borrowed.
Running long: cut to fit with room for pauses; a speaker who breaks down needs slack.
Unchecked facts: a wrong grandchild's name or year is remembered. Verify every name with the family twice.
A string of borrowed quotations: one verse or saying the person actually loved means more.
cards.exemplar_brief: Eulogy to be read by a granddaughter at the shraddhanjali sabha in Indore for her grandfather, a retired government-school headmaster who played the harmonium; the room is family, former students and neighbours; Hinglish leaning Hindi, in Roman script, written for her to read aloud; 450-600 words; goal: the room recognises him in the stories and leaves with a memory to keep.

verified.note: Feels like a real granddaughter speaking. Natural Roman Hinglish leaning Hindi, written in breath lines. Three distinct stories show different sides (the sticking harmonium key with 'ungli ki jaldbaazi', fees paid quietly from salary, the watch ten minutes fast as affectionate humour). There is a lovely callback farewell, thanks to the room and a fitting 'Om Shanti'. Stand-in stories and names are flagged for the family to confirm, as the brief gives none. Nit: 'Hedmaster' should be spelled 'Headmaster'.

cards.name: Event promotion & invitation copy
cards.summary: Copy that fills seats or sells tickets: the event page, invitation, social posts, reminders and last-call messages. Good event copy puts what, who it is for, why attend, when, where and price in the first screen, backs it with proof (named speakers, past attendees), and moves the reader to register before a real deadline.
use_for: Conference and summit event pages
Webinar invitations and reminder emails
Workshop, comedy or concert ticket pages
Corporate and community invitations (launches, meetups, felicitations)
Reminder and last-call WhatsApp and SMS messages
avoid: Leading with the agenda or the organiser's history: lead with what the attendee gets.
Fake scarcity ('Only 5 seats left!' for an empty hall): a dark pattern; use real deadlines such as early-bird end or registration close.
Missing logistics (time zone, venue directions, session language, refunds): people drop off at the last step.
The post-event write-up: that is genre:event_recap_post.

sources.title: AWAI: 80 In-Demand Copywriting Projects (updated 2026-02-02)
sources.supports: lists 'Event Materials' and 'Trade Show Materials' as priced project types

sources.title: Eventbrite: Ultimate guide to copywriting for events
sources.supports: ticketing platform guide to event pages, invitations and promo emails

cards.value_why: AWAI's 2026 pricing guide lists 'Event Materials' and 'Trade Show Materials' as project types, and ticketing platforms such as Eventbrite publish event-copywriting guides for organisers. Steady demand, usually bundled with event marketing.
cards.goal: Register or buy a ticket before the deadline, and then actually show up.

structure.does: The payoff or experience, not just the event name ('File your own ITR in one Saturday morning').
Date, time with time zone, venue or online format, price, language, who it is for.
Specific takeaways or experiences in benefit terms.
Names with a one-line credential; real past-attendee numbers or quotes.
Session titles that each promise something specific.
One button with price or 'free' and the deadline; what happens after registering (confirmation, calendar invite, joining link).
Parking, accessibility, refunds, recording, dress code.
Confirmation, day-before reminder, hour-before reminder with link or directions, last call for unsold seats.

length.note: An event page runs a few hundred words; invitations, posts and reminders are short. Ticket price and travel effort decide how much persuasion the page needs.

checklist: Are date, time (with time zone if online), venue or format and price all in the first screen?
Does the headline promise a specific payoff or experience?
Does it say who the event is for?
Are speakers or performers named with a credential?
Is there one registration CTA, worded the same each time it appears?
Is every deadline or seat limit real?
Does it say what happens after registering?
Are refunds, recording and accessibility covered?
Do reminders include the joining link or venue directions?
pitfalls: Session titles that say nothing ('Panel discussion', 'Fireside chat'): name the question each session answers.
Stock adjectives ('exciting', 'insightful', 'power-packed'): replace with what attendees will leave with.
Time-zone slips for online events with NRI or global audiences: state IST plus the one or two zones most of the audience uses.
Email invites pasted into WhatsApp: rewrite short, with the link and one line of why; commercial WhatsApp messages need opt-in and an approved template.
Free events with high no-shows: remind people what they will miss and make the calendar invite one tap.
cards.exemplar_brief: Event page plus a 3-message WhatsApp reminder sequence for a Saturday-morning in-person workshop in Indore, 'File your own ITR in 3 hours', run by a local CA firm for salaried professionals aged 25-40; Rs 499 ticket, 40 seats, early-bird price until a stated date; English for the page, Hinglish for WhatsApp; page 350-550 words, reminders 40-80 words each; goal: buy a ticket and attend.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Round 1's season error is fixed: Saturday 10 July 2027, before the 31 July due date, early bird to Saturday 26 June, reminder on Friday 9 July (weekdays all correct). Payoff headline, key facts up top, four benefit bullets, a time-boxed agenda ending in e-verification, one CTA worded the same each time, what happens after booking, an opt-in line, the never-share-your-OTP FAQ, and three natural Hinglish reminders (62-67 words) with the checklist, a login check, parking and a gate contact. Nits (writer): 'Rs 499 until 26 June, then [regular price]' reads the brief's Rs 499 as the early-bird price, which the brief leaves ambiguous; 'Seats sirf 40 hain, isliye samay par aaiye' is a non-sequitur. | round 1: weak 7

cards.name: Event recap post
cards.summary: An article or social post published soon after a conference, launch or meetup that gives people who missed it the two or three takeaways that matter, with attributed quotes, numbers and photos, and gives attendees something to share. Good recaps are organised by insight, not agenda order, and include the writer's first-hand observations.
use_for: Company blog or LinkedIn recap of a conference the team hosted or attended
Community meetup or hackathon recap
Product-launch event recap for the press page
Internal recap of an offsite or town hall
Takeaways thread or carousel
avoid: Agenda replay ('First X spoke about... then Y...'): lead with the takeaways and group them by theme.
Quotes from memory or unchecked auto-transcripts: verify against the recording, and get speaker approval when the brief asks for it.
Publishing weeks later: recaps are timely; publish while attendees are still talking about it.
Turning it into a sales pitch: one closing line about the client, at most.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
sources.supports: asks whether content provides original information or reporting and demonstrates first-hand expertise, and flags content that mainly summarises what others say

cards.value_why: No dedicated marketplace category found on 2026-10-04; produced in-house by marketing teams or bundled into event coverage. Its worth is first-hand material, the kind Google's people-first content guidance asks for.
cards.goal: Get the key takeaways in a few minutes and, if they missed it, want to attend next time.

structure.does: The biggest takeaway or a number, plus the event name.
What, when, where and who in one or two sentences, then why it mattered.
Two to five insights, each with a subhead, a supporting quote or data point attributed to a named speaker, and the writer's own observation.
One or two specific scenes (a demo, a debate, an audience question), with captioned photos.
Links to recordings and slides, the next event date, a soft CTA.

length.note: A social recap is a few hundred words; a blog recap runs longer. The number of real takeaways decides it, not the length of the agenda.

checklist: Does the opening give the main takeaway rather than the agenda?
Is every quote attributed to a named speaker and checked against the recording or notes?
Does each takeaway carry a specific number, example or quote?
Is there at least one first-hand observation from the writer?
Are takeaways grouped by theme rather than session order?
Are links to recordings or slides included where they exist?
Are the event name, date and place in the first paragraph?
Is promotion of the client limited to a short closing line?
pitfalls: 'It was an amazing event with insightful sessions' openers: delete and start with the insight.
Misquotes: paraphrase when unsure, and flag quotes awaiting speaker approval.
Photo captions without names: caption who and what, and get permission for close-ups of attendees.
Hinglish community recaps are fine, but keep speaker names, titles and numbers exact.
cards.exemplar_brief: Company-blog recap by 'LedgerLoop' (demo name), a Bengaluru B2B SaaS startup, of 'Fintech Product Night', a meetup it hosted for founders and product managers who missed it; English; 600-900 words; goal: readers get the takeaways and sign up for the next meetup. Event notes (speaker approvals received, quotes may be used verbatim): Thursday 24 September 2026, 6:30-9 pm, a co-working space in Indiranagar, Bengaluru; 140 registered, 96 attended. (1) Neha Rao, head of product at a payments company: 'We moved the autopay explainer before the PIN screen, and first-debit failures fell from 17% to 9% in two months.' (2) Imran Qureshi, risk lead at a lending startup: 40% of KYC drop-offs happen at the selfie step; a retry with on-screen guidance cut them by a third. (3) Deepa Menon, founder of a Kochi invoice-discounting startup: 'Only 3 of 10 small businesses ask about the rate; 9 of 10 ask on which day the money lands.' (4) Arjun Sethi, product manager at a neobank: Hindi and Kannada screens lifted Tier 2 activation from 31% to 38%. Scene: Imran's live demo froze for 30 seconds on the venue Wi-Fi; he switched to his phone hotspot and the room clapped when it loaded. Recording: youtu.be/demo-recap and slides at ledgerloop.example/slides (demo links). Next meetup: Thursday 5 November 2026.

verified.note: Opens on the takeaway rather than the agenda. Four themed takeaways each have a quote slot marked pending approval and a crisp 'My take'. There is a scene, recording and slides links, and a single sign-up CTA; the draft note forbids publishing unapproved quotes. Deductions: the headline names compliance, but that is takeaway 3, not the lead. The scene contains an unmarked invented direct quote ('it depends who picks up the phone') and invented audience behaviour, attributed to a panelist. The brief gave no event content, so the takeaways themselves are stand-ins. cards.name: Executive summary
cards.summary: A one-to-two-page standalone summary at the front of a report, proposal or plan that lets a decision-maker act without reading the rest. Good executive summaries lead with the recommendation or ask, give the reasons and key numbers behind it, state cost, risk and timeline, and are written last so they match the document exactly.
use_for: Front of a business plan, feasibility study or research report
Proposal or RFP response summary
Board or management paper
Consulting or audit deliverable
Grant proposal summary
avoid: Writing an introduction ('This report examines...'): state the finding and the recommendation.
Teasing ('Read on to learn...'): it must stand alone; nothing the decision needs may be missing, and nothing may appear that the body doesn't support.
Background first: one or two sentences of context at most, then the answer.
A one-page sales leave-behind: that is genre:one_pager.
