cards.goal: Make the decision (approve, fund, choose), or know exactly what is being asked, after reading only the summary.

structure.does: The recommendation, finding or ask, with the headline number (cost, return, saving).
The situation and problem, only as much as the decision needs.
Usually three points supporting the recommendation, each with its evidence number.
structure.length: 3 bullets or short paragraphs, 30-60 words each

structure.does: The alternatives and why they lose, a line each.
What it takes, what could go wrong with its mitigation, and key dates.
Exactly what the reader must decide or approve, and by when.

length.note: One page for most documents, two at most for long reports. Past two pages it has become a second report.

checklist: Is the recommendation or ask in the first two sentences?
Could a reader decide without opening the full document?
Is every number identical to the corresponding number in the body?
Is every finding in the summary supported in the body?
Are cost, risk and timeline stated?
Does it end with the decision required and a date?
Is it free of 'This report will...' and 'read on' phrasing?
Does it fit on one page (two at most)?
Is jargon defined or removed for a non-specialist decision-maker?
pitfalls: Written first and never updated: write it last, then re-check every number against the final body.
Hedging on every line ('may potentially', 'could possibly'): state the confidence level once, then write cleanly.
Narrating the process ('We conducted 24 interviews and analysed...'): one clause of method, then results.
Nominalisations ('implementation of the optimisation of...'): turn nouns back into verbs (tech:unhide_verbs).
Indian boards often read on phones: short paragraphs, the ask in bold, lakh/crore used consistently (lang:india_locale_formats).
cards.exemplar_brief: Executive summary for a feasibility report recommending that a Nagpur dairy cooperative invest Rs 4.2 crore in a solar-powered bulk milk-chilling network across 12 villages; readers are the cooperative's board; English; 350-500 words, one page; goal: the board approves phase 1 at its meeting on Thursday 12 November 2026. Report findings to carry (all figures are in the body): collection is 24,000 litres a day across the 12 villages; spoilage and rejection are 6.0% now (1,440 litres a day) and would fall to 1.5% (360 litres), saving 1,080 litres a day; at an average procurement price of Rs 34 a litre that is Rs 1.34 crore a year; annual operation and maintenance costs Rs 18 lakh, so the net saving is Rs 1.16 crore a year and payback is 3.6 years. Funding mix for Rs 4.2 crore: 40% state dairy-development grant (applied for, Rs 1.68 crore), 35% bank loan (Rs 1.47 crore), 25% the cooperative's own funds (Rs 1.05 crore). Phase 1 is 5 villages at Rs 1.75 crore, installed within 5 months of approval and before summer 2027; phase 2 is 7 villages at Rs 2.45 crore. Options considered: grid-powered chillers (Rs 3.3 crore, plus Rs 31 lakh a year in power, and daily outages in 4 villages) and doing nothing (6.0% spoilage continues). Main risk: grant release is delayed; mitigation: phase 1 can be funded from the loan and own funds alone.

verified.note: Recommendation and bolded ask come in the first two sentences. Phase 1 is sized as one-third of villages and money (4 villages, Rs 1.4 crore of 4.2), which reconciles, and the three reasons are well chosen. Options are ranked with a reason each, every risk has a mitigation, and it ends with the exact decision and tender authority. No 'this report will'. Deductions: the bottom line carries only the cost, not the return or payback the card's 'Bottom line' asks for (a placeholder belonged there). Every decision number is a placeholder because the brief supplies no report findings. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> state the report's headline findings (current spoilage percent, annual saving in Rs lakh, payback in years, funding mix) so the summary can carry the numbers a board decides on. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now states the report's headline findings (spoilage %, annual saving, payback, funding mix, phasing, options, risk) with reconciled arithmetic and a dated decision; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Expert roundup post
cards.summary: An article built from short answers by several named experts to one sharp question, grouped into themes, with the writer's synthesis of where they agree, where they disagree and what the reader should do. Good roundups use real, permissioned, attributed quotes from people with first-hand experience of the question; the synthesis is the product.
use_for: SEO and thought-leadership posts ('7 D2C founders on the one change that cut their CAC')
Annual predictions or trends pieces
Relationship-building with industry voices ahead of PR or partnerships
A newsletter section or carousel of expert tips
avoid: A list of quotes with no synthesis: add themes, a verdict and a takeaway.
Fabricated, AI-generated or 'adapted' quotes: every quote comes from the named person, with permission. Invented quotes deceive readers and expose the client.
Experts picked for follower count: pick practitioners who have done the thing.
Questions too broad ('What's the future of marketing?'): ask a specific question that draws different, concrete answers.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
sources.supports: asks whether content provides original information and first-hand expertise, and whether it mainly summarises what others say without adding much value

buyers: Content-marketing teams at SaaS and B2B companies
cards.value_why: No dedicated marketplace category found on 2026-10-04; produced in-house or bundled into link-building and PR-led content. Real expert input is the original, first-hand material Google's helpful-content guidance asks for, which keeps the format useful as AI summaries commoditise generic posts.
cards.goal: Take away a clear, multi-source answer to the question, act on the synthesised advice, and see the publisher as the one who convened the experts.

structure.does: Number of experts plus the specific question or outcome.
Why the question matters now, who was asked and how they were chosen, the exact question, and the one-line headline finding.
The three or four patterns across answers, where experts disagreed, and the writer's verdict.
Each: name, role, organisation, link; the quote edited for length only, with approval; a one-line takeaway from the writer.
A checklist or next steps distilled from the answers.
How and when quotes were gathered, disclosure of any commercial relationships, then a CTA (subscribe, share).

length.note: The expert count drives it: 5-8 experts make a tight post, 15+ a long resource. Cap quote length rather than cutting experts.

checklist: Is every quote attributed to a named person with role and organisation?
Has every expert approved their quote, or is it clearly marked pending approval?
Does the intro state the exact question asked and how experts were chosen?
Is there a synthesis that names agreements, disagreements and a verdict?
Are answers grouped by theme rather than alphabet or fame?
Does each answer add something no other answer said?
Are paid or commercial relationships with featured experts disclosed?
Is there a practical takeaway list at the end?
pitfalls: Ten experts saying the same thing: cut duplicates or merge them in one line ('Four founders said...').
Over-edited quotes that no longer sound like the person: edit for length and clarity only, then send back for approval.
Self-promotional answers: ask experts for an example from their own work, and trim product plugs.
A narrow panel: for an Indian audience, include voices beyond the big metros and a mix of genders where the topic allows.
'Roundups' stitched from public quotes or AI: that is the scaled, low-value pattern search spam policies target. Collect original answers.
cards.exemplar_brief: Expert roundup for a Mumbai D2C growth agency's blog: '7 Indian D2C founders on the one change that cut their customer acquisition cost', for early-stage D2C founders; the writer drafts the intro, synthesis and takeaways and edits the answers; English; 1,200-1,800 words; goal: readers apply one tactic and subscribe to the agency's newsletter. Interview notes (demo founders, interviewed 14-25 September 2026, quotes approved; each gave one change, CAC before and after, and the approved quote shown): (1) Aditi Sharma, founder, skincare, Delhi: customer unboxing videos instead of studio shots; Rs 820 to Rs 560 in 3 months. Approved quote: 'A studio shot shows what we want people to think. A customer unboxing shows what actually arrives, and that is what made strangers trust us.' (2) Rohan Iyer, co-founder, coffee, Chennai: Rs 49 sampling sachet as the first order; Rs 640 to Rs 410 in 2 months. Approved quote: 'Nobody wants to pay full price for coffee they have never tasted. A Rs 49 sachet as the first order lets them taste it first, so the full bag stops being a gamble.' (3) Fatima Khan, founder, modest fashion, Hyderabad: WhatsApp cart recovery within 30 minutes; Rs 950 to Rs 780 in 6 weeks. Approved quote: 'Most carts die in the first hour. A WhatsApp nudge at 30 minutes brought back more buyers than any new ad we ran.' (4) Karan Malhotra, founder, protein snacks, Pune: cut Meta ads to 3 broad audiences; Rs 710 to Rs 520 in 8 weeks. Approved quote: 'Slicing audiences made us feel precise, not profitable. With three broad audiences, the creative does the targeting.' (5) Sneha Pillai, founder, baby care, Kochi: 5% prepaid discount; Rs 880 to Rs 700 (after returns) in 10 weeks. Approved quote: 'Offering 5% off for paying upfront moved buyers to prepaid. I count CAC after returns, because a sale that comes back is not a customer.' (6) Vikram Rathore, co-founder, ethnic menswear, Jaipur: founder-led Instagram Lives twice a week; Rs 1,050 to Rs 730 in 4 months. Approved quote: 'Twice a week I go live, show the kurtas and answer questions as they come. People buy from someone they have watched, not from an ad they scrolled past.' (7) Nisha Deshpande, founder, pet food, Nagpur: free gift instead of 20% off on the first order; Rs 760 to Rs 540 in 6 weeks. Approved quote: 'A 20% discount trains people to wait for the next sale. A free gift on the first order felt like a welcome, and our CAC came down.' Disagreement to use: Karan says creative beats targeting; Fatima says fixing after the click beats any ad change. Disclosure: Aditi and Rohan are clients of the agency.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. Uses all seven notes correctly; every cut checks (36, 32, 30, 29, 27, 20, 18%); the client disclosure appears in the intro, at each client's answer and in the method note; the Karan/Fatima disagreement gets a cautious verdict; themes, a numbers table, start-by-situation advice and takeaways follow (round 1's denominator slip is fixed). But the seven answers are '[Approved quote, 25-40 words]' slots, so no expert speaks and the answers section reads as the table restated seven times. Nit (writer): Karan's audience cut sits under 'Change what people see', which it is not. Fault: card (the brief says 'quotes approved' and asks the writer to edit the answers, but supplies no answer text). CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> after each founder's note add the approved quote itself, one or two sentences in the founder's voice (e.g. Fatima: 'Most carts die in the first hour. A WhatsApp nudge at 30 minutes brought back more buyers than any new ad we ran.'), so the answers can be edited rather than left as slots. | round 1: weak 7 | CARD FIXED 2026-10-13 (lead fix5): exemplar_brief now carries each founder's approved quote after the note; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Explainer video script
cards.summary: A short VO script, usually 60-120 seconds, that explains a product, idea or process in an order a viewer can follow: the problem they recognise, how it works in simple steps, what they get, and one action. Good explainers carry one metaphor or visual idea, write every line for the ear with its visual beside it, and cut everything that doesn't serve the single message.
use_for: SaaS or app product explainer for a homepage or store listing
Government scheme or process explainer (how to apply)
Fintech or insurance concept explainer ('How term insurance works')
Internal process or policy explainer
Short-form explainer reels
avoid: Feature tours: pick the two or three features that solve the stated problem.
Narration written without visuals: use a two-column script so every line has a picture.
Paid placements: once it sells in a paid slot it is an ad (genre:video_ad_script) and ad codes apply.
Long-form teaching: past a few minutes it becomes genre:youtube_video_script or genre:elearning_course_script.

cards.goal: Understand how the product or idea works and take the one next step (sign up, download, apply, message).

structure.does: The viewer's problem in a relatable moment, in the opening seconds.
Why the problem matters: cost, time or risk.
Names the product or idea and its promise in one line.
Three simple steps or one extended metaphor, each line paired with a visual.
What changes for the viewer; one number or customer line.
One action, said aloud and shown on screen (URL, app name, number).

length.note: VO words. 60-120 seconds is a craft convention, not a sourced limit; confirm the duration with the client and budget words from a timed read-aloud at the narrator's pace, leaving pauses for visuals.

checklist: Does the script state the viewer's problem in the first two lines?
Is it in two columns with a visual for every VO line?
Does it explain how it works in three steps or fewer, or through one metaphor?
Is there exactly one CTA, both said and shown?
Does a timed read-aloud fit the agreed duration with room for pauses?
Is on-screen text shorter than the VO and not a word-for-word repeat?
Are claims (savings, speed, numbers) provable?
Is jargon replaced or explained in one line?
Would a viewer with the sound off still get the message from on-screen text?
pitfalls: Opening with the company ('At XYZ, we believe...'): open with the viewer's moment.
Too many messages: if the client wants five features explained, propose a short series instead.
Hindi or Hinglish VO in English word order: write it as people speak and test it with the narrator or TTS (lang:hindi_voiceover_tts).
Metaphors that need explaining: test the metaphor on someone outside the industry first.
Visuals the budget can't make: ask for the style frame first and describe shots the studio or AI tool can actually produce.
cards.exemplar_brief: 90-second animated explainer for a Pune agritech app that lets small farmers book a soil test and receive a fertiliser plan on WhatsApp; audience: farmers in Maharashtra and their smartphone-savvy children; Hindi (Devanagari) VO, two-column script (visual | VO + on-screen text); 180-240 words of VO; goal: viewers send 'Hi' to the WhatsApp number shown on screen.

verified.note: Opens on the farmer's moment ('Papa, kabhi mitti se poocha hai?') with stakes in money and yield. The product and promise come in one line, then a doctor-pulse metaphor and exactly three steps (book on WhatsApp, sample pickup, plan with which fertiliser, how much, when), each paired with a visual. A proof slot follows, and one CTA ('Hi bhejiye') is said and shown. Spoken Hindi is natural and the VO fits 90 seconds. Deductions: every on-screen text line ends in a stray full stop ('fasal wahi?.'); 'hamara aadmi' should be 'hamare karyakarta'; 'baba' fits rural Maharashtra better than 'papa'.
